opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we spent a lot of time thinking about. The core idea behind Genie was that we wanted to learn from video, and the overwhelming majority of video on the internet doesn't come with action labels. You have millions of hours of people playing games, but you don't know what buttons they pressed. So the question became: can we infer a notion of action purely from how frames change over time?

That's where the latent action model comes in. We learn a small, discrete set of latent actions, in the original work just eight, that explain the transition from one frame to the next. And that choice embeds a few assumptions. One is that the meaningful variation between consecutive frames can be captured by a small, discrete vocabulary. That works surprisingly well for platformer-style games, where you're mostly moving left, right, jumping, and so on. It also makes the model playable, because a person can map those latent codes to keys and actually control the generated world.

But it's definitely a simplification. Real control spaces can be continuous, high-dimensional, or compositional. Think about a robot arm, or a game where you're aiming and moving at the same time. A tiny discrete codebook isn't going to capture all of that. There's also an assumption that the changes between frames are mostly caused by the agent, when in reality lots of things in a scene move on their own: other characters, the environment, camera motion. The model has to disentangle what the controllable agent did from everything else, and it doesn't always do that perfectly.

So I think of the action space as a useful inductive bias rather than ground truth. Keeping it small and discrete forces the model to find the most consistent, controllable factors of variation, which is exactly what you want for something interactive. And what was exciting to us is that those latent actions ended up being semantically consistent across very different environments, so "this code means move right" tended to hold even in games the model had never seen. Going forward, I'm really interested in how we relax those assumptions, richer or continuous action spaces, and ways to ground latent actions in real actions when you do have a bit of labeled data, especially for things like robotics, where the gap between "what changed in the video" and "what the agent actually did" matters a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says the small, discrete latent codes make Genie playable because a person can map them to keys to control the generated world.

r002.rationale: The response says latent actions were semantically consistent across different environments, but does not explain that assuming a common action space across training environments enables Genie to learn a general action representation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core assumption in Genie is that there's a small, discrete set of actions that can explain what changes between consecutive frames in a video. We never have ground-truth action labels, right? We're training purely on unlabeled internet video of people playing 2D platformers, so the latent action model has to infer what the "action" was from the transition itself. And we constrain that to a small codebook, eight codes in the paper, through a VQ bottleneck.

The reason that's a reasonable assumption for the domain we chose is that platformers really do have a small number of things the player can do. Left, right, jump, maybe a couple more. So forcing the model to compress the frame-to-frame change into one of a handful of tokens pushes it toward something that looks like controls, rather than just encoding everything that happened in the frame. If you made the codebook huge, the model would just cheat and stuff the entire next frame into the latent action, and then it's not an action anymore, it's a copy of the future.

But I want to be honest about where that assumption gets strained. There's an implicit assumption that most of the change in a frame is attributable to the agent. In a platformer that's mostly true, but there are enemies moving, there's background parallax, there's camera motion. Some of that leaks into the latent actions. And the model has no notion of which entity is "you." It just learns whatever consistent transformation explains the data. So when we looked at the learned codes, they were semantically consistent across games, which was really exciting, but you could also see codes that were doing some mix of character motion and something else.

The other thing is the discreteness itself. Real action spaces in robotics are continuous, and when we did the robotics experiments we were still mapping onto a discrete codebook. That worked better than I expected, honestly, but it means we're quantizing a space that doesn't want to be quantized, and the right answer there probably involves either more codes or a different kind of bottleneck.

And then there's the temporal assumption. We're saying one action per frame transition at a fixed frame rate. If the actual control happens at a different timescale than the video, you're smearing actions across steps, or compressing several into one. I think of the action space less as a claim about how the world works and more as an inductive bias we chose because it made the problem tractable and it gave us something controllable at the end. The interesting research question is how much you can relax it before the thing stops being a playable, controllable world model.

r001.rationale: It says the small codebook makes the model's learned tokens resemble controls and describes the result as controllable, indicating the restriction supports easier interaction.

r002.rationale: It says learned codes were semantically consistent across games, but does not explain that a shared action space across training environments enables a general action representation.

astra-6.text:
I think the key assumption is that there’s a relatively small set of actions that explains how the environment changes, and that you can infer those actions from video. Genie doesn’t get action labels, so it learns a latent action space—a compressed representation of the transition between frames—and then uses that to condition the world model.

The interesting question is whether those latent actions correspond to things an agent can actually control. In a platformer, moving left or right gives you a fairly clear connection between an action and a visual change. But a video can also change because the camera moves or something else in the environment moves. So learning a representation that predicts those changes isn’t necessarily the same as discovering the agent’s actions.

That’s where I’d be careful about generalizing the assumption. It’s useful for learning a controllable model from unlabeled video, but whether that action space maps onto the actions available to a real agent is a separate question.

r001.rationale: The response describes a relatively small latent action set, but does not say the action space was restricted to make interaction with Genie easier.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that training environments share a common action space or that this lets Genie learn a general action representation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key assumption is that you can describe the changes you see in a video with a relatively small, discrete set of actions. Genie doesn’t get action labels, so it has to learn a latent action space—essentially, a representation of what could have caused one frame to change into the next.

That’s useful because you can learn from video without knowing which buttons someone pressed. But there’s a question of what those latent actions actually capture. Is it the character moving, the camera moving, or something else in the scene? Those can all produce visual change, but they don’t necessarily correspond to things an agent can control.

So I’d distinguish learning a useful interface for generating video from learning the action space of an embodied agent. For the latter, you want actions to have consistent meanings and predictable effects across situations. That’s a stronger requirement than producing a plausible next frame.

r001.rationale: The response describes a small discrete latent action set, but does not say Genie’s action space was restricted to make interaction with the model easier.

r002.rationale: It discusses consistent action meanings across situations as a desirable property, but does not explain that a common action space across training environments lets Genie learn a general action representation.
